## Definition

**Dispersion** (also called spread or variability) describes how spread out the values in a dataset are around the central tendency (mean or median).

## Why Dispersion Matters

Two datasets can have the same mean but very different spreads:

```
Dataset A: 48, 49, 50, 51, 52    Mean = 50, Low spread
Dataset B: 10, 30, 50, 70, 90    Mean = 50, High spread
```

Reporting the mean alone is incomplete without a measure of dispersion.

## Measures of Dispersion

| Measure | Formula | Best For |
|---------|---------|----------|
| Range | Max - Min | Quick overview |
| Interquartile Range | Q3 - Q1 | Ordinal data, outliers present |
| Variance | Mean squared deviation | Mathematical calculations |
| Standard Deviation | √Variance | Most common, same units as data |

## Visual Comparison

```
Low Dispersion          High Dispersion
    ▲ █ ▲                    ▲
    ███                    ▲   ▲
   █████                 ▲       ▲
  ███████              ▲           ▲
─────┼─────          ─────┼─────
   Mean                  Mean
```

## Choosing a Measure

| Data Type | Recommended |
|-----------|-------------|
| Interval/ratio, normal | Standard deviation |
| Ordinal or skewed | Interquartile range |
| Quick description | Range |

## R Code Example

```r
# Range
range(scores)
diff(range(scores))

# IQR
IQR(scores)

# Standard deviation
sd(scores)

# Variance
var(scores)

# Summary statistics
summary(scores)
```

## Reporting

Always report a measure of dispersion with central tendency:

> Reaction times had a mean of 450 ms (*SD* = 52).

> Ratings had a median of 4 (*IQR* = 2).

## DataLab Connection

When reporting DataLab results, always include a measure of dispersion. High dispersion in reaction times at **Reflex Test** suggests large individual differences in processing speed.
